text.p: Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and his Islamist Welfare Party have shattered secular Turkey's taboo on religion-based politics, but the party faithful close out 1996 with little else to show for their hard-won victory.
Erbakan fashioned a slim election win a year ago with support from a potent political cocktail of Islamists and the economically disaffected left behind in Turkey's modernisation.
Six months later he cut a coalition deal with a right-wing party to become the first Islamist to lead Turkey in its 73 years as an officially secular republic.

But failure so far to deliver for the masses or make good on an explicit Islamist social agenda has frustrated many of his followers and clouded the prospects for Erbakan's tenure, scheduled to expire in mid-1998.
"We cannot say that Welfare has had any real success in political terms in this six-month period," said analyst and commentator Ali Bayramoglu.
"Welfare, as a protest against the system, has limited room to manoeuvre. So far it has not even entered that arena, disappointing its grassroots voters," Bayramoglu told Reuters.
Recent opinion polls have suggested a downturn in support for Welfare, which narrowly won general elections last December with just 21 percent of the vote in a crowded field.
Inflation remains rampant, at about 80 percent, and ballooning budget deficits have driven borrowing costs to dizzying heights.

There is no sign to date of a serious attempt to take on the powerful "rentier class" -- disparaged throughout the campaign as slothful coupon clippers -- or to introduce Welfare's millenarian "Just Order" of economic and social equality.
PAY RISE FOR CIVIL SERVANTS

Instead, Erbakan's voters have had to make do with a one-off pay rise for civil servants, a common ploy of incoming prime ministers, and high-profile foreign visits to Islamic countries -- including a controversial visit to Libya -- in place of the usual tour of Western capitals.
They have even watched in dismay as he preached the fiscal discipline of a proposed "zero deficit" budget and championed swift privatisation with all the zeal of the newly converted.

Top foreign policy promises -- an end to growing ties to Israel and expulsion of a Western air force patrolling Iraq from a base in Turkey -- were quickly dropped. A vow to smother the Kurdish insurgency in "Moslem fellowship" has gone nowhere.
"Welfare's DNA make-up includes a line protesting against the system, but in practice it cannot realise this," Islamist intellectual Ahmet Tasgetiren told the daily Yeni Yuzyil.
"It shares power but does not make any effort to give life to this protest," he said.

Swelling disappointment among Welfare voters appears to justify the private reservations of Erbakan aides about taking power in coalition with the free-market conservatives of the True Path Party of Tansu Ciller, the former prime minister.
It also risks a militant backlash. Already, Erbakan has had to wade into party politics to block more radical members from coming to the fore.
Better to remain in opposition and build electoral strength, some aides argued, then to enter a coalition with the pro-Western True Path.
TOP PRIZE FINALLY SEIZED
In the end, the veteran politico won out over the long-term visionary: the 70-year-old party boss was not prepared to let the top prize elude him any longer.

"Erbakan had no choice. The rank-and-file demanded he take power," said newspaper editor and columnist Ilnur Cevik, who credits the prime minister with engineering a "soft landing" amid the hostility of the ruling elite, especially the army.
"The myth that the military would never allow Welfare to come to power -- that myth has been exploded," said Cevik, an Erbakan confidant and editor of the Turkish Daily News.

Cevik argues Erbakan has also come to dominate coalition partner Ciller, under a cloud of corruption allegations, eliminating any need for early polls in 1997. But he admits Welfare may be running out of time with ordinary voters.
"The real crunch will come when the people who supported Welfare will start asking for results," something he says lies ahead in the first half of 1997.
Erbakan's lacklustre record contrasts sharply with the effective urban management that Welfare mayors have introduced lately in many leading cities, including Istanbul and Ankara.
Success at the local level at rooting out petty corruption and improving city services has attracted broad support, even among secularists.
These municipal leaders have also succeeded in channelling more funds to Islamic education facilities and neighbourhood mosques, securing their political base among the pious.
Applying that formula to Turkey as a whole, say analysts, is the key to any success Erbakan may enjoy in 1997.
"Welfare has the tools and it has the experience of good urban government," said one Western diplomat.
"Does it have the will to break the (national) system it was elected to replace?" he asked.
